title: Communicating Honestly in Times of Uncertainty
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Admired Leadership offers a six-part script for leaders who must address a team during uncertain times. The argument is that honest communication requires structure, so that candor does not slide into sugarcoating, guardedness or false confidence. The piece moves step by step through what is known, what is not known, a commitment to share future news, a specific ask of the team, an invitation to questions and an expression of thanks. Its central claim is that this structure lets leaders calm anxiety and redirect attention to what people can control. The post closes by tying openness to credibility and trust.
points: Telling people explicitly what is not yet known reassures them that the leader is not withholding critical information.
Leaders should commit publicly to sharing news as soon as they learn it, even if that promise cannot always be kept perfectly.
Asking for one specific action gives anxious team members something they control and prevents paralysis.
Inviting questions is valuable even when the leader has no answers, because it lets people air what is on their minds.
Ending with appreciation cements the honesty and openness the leader is trying to build.
quotes: Uncertain times create stress and anxiety for everyone impacted by an unpredictable future. The challenge for leaders is to communicate with confidence and honesty while downplaying their own fears and predictions about what might transpire.
This is what we know right now. Don’t sugarcoat or protect people from the truth. Tell them exactly where things stand with what we know at the moment.

This is what we don’t know. Team members will always wonder if the leader is holding back or protecting them from critical information. By telling people what isn’t known, leaders reassure them this isn’t the case.
Here is my commitment to you going forward. Strong leaders publicly declare they will share what they learn as soon as they learn it.

This is what I would like you to do. Good leaders refuse to allow the uncertainty to paralyze the team. They know asking for a specific action from team members helps to alleviate anxiety and focuses their attention on what they do control.
Uncertainty is difficult for everyone. Leaders who make the choice to communicate openly with the team are typically rewarded with credibility and trust.
